sections.html:
Trumbull is a Fairfield County town in the Greater Bridgeport Planning Region, bordering Bridgeport, Shelton, Stratford, Fairfield, Easton and Monroe. It had 36,827 residents at the 2020 census and covers 23.5 square miles.

The land runs from about 40 feet above sea level at Beach Park to 615 feet at the top of Monitor Hill, so a house may stand on level ground near the Pequonnock River or on a hillside lot. The two sell differently, and buyers will ask about grading and drainage on the second kind.

The big population jump came after the war: 8,641 people in 1950, 20,379 in 1960 and 31,394 in 1970. A good share of the houses likely date from those decades. Your deed and the assessor's record show the year yours was built. Knowing it helps you answer questions about wiring, windows and the heating system before a buyer raises them.

Trumbull is a town of villages and has no single downtown. They are Trumbull Center, Long Hill, Nichols, Daniels Farm and Tashua. The Nichols Farms Historic District and the Christ Episcopal Church and Tashua Burial Ground are on the National Register, so if your house is within the Nichols Farms district, ask the town what that means for exterior changes before you plan work.

Green space is a real selling point. The town has 871.23 acres of park facilities, including Twin Brooks Park, Indian Ledge Park and Robert G. Beach Memorial Park, along with the 382-acre Pequonnock River Valley State Park and the 268-acre Tashua Recreation Facility with its golf course. If your house sits near a park or trail, say so.

RouteWhat it does in Trumbull
Route 8Freeway through the southeast part of town toward Waterbury and Interstate 84
Route 15 (Merritt Parkway)Runs east to New Haven and west toward New York City
Route 25North to south, joins Route 8 at the Bridgeport line
Route 108Nichols Avenue and Huntington Turnpike, north from Stratford
Route 111Main Street, from Bridgeport's North End to Monroe
Route 127White Plains Road and Church Hill Road through the town center

No Metro-North station is in town. The closest are Bridgeport at 4.6 miles, Stratford at 4.9 and Fairfield-Black Rock at 5.7, all on the New Haven Line. Greater Bridgeport Transit Authority runs the buses. Buyers who commute care about that distance, so state it.

Trumbull Public Schools has Trumbull High School, two middle schools (Hillcrest and Madison) and six elementary schools: Booth Hill, Daniels Farm, Frenchtown, Jane Ryan, Middlebrook and Tashua. Families will want to know which one serves the address.

Fire protection comes from three all-volunteer departments: the Long Hill Fire District, the Nichols Fire District and the Trumbull Center Fire District. Each handles its own tax structure and fundraising, so your tax bill may include a district line. Check the current bill or ask the tax collector, and tell the buyer.

Westfield Trumbull mall sits on Route 111 at the Bridgeport line, and an office park north of the Merritt Parkway near the Shelton and Stratford borders has housed firms such as UnitedHealthcare. Planning rules include professional office overlay zones along White Plains Road, Church Hill Road and Main Street, and a mixed-use zone around the historic Long Hill Green. If you own property along those corridors, confirm current zoning with the town.

Trumbull's deed gets recorded with the town clerk, and Connecticut Form OP-236 travels with it. The grantor, the grantor's lawyer or an agent signs it, and both the return and any tax fall due on the recording date. Trumbull's town code is 144.

The tax reaches any deed with consideration of $2,000 or more. Where the town participates in myCTREC the return goes in online. Elsewhere it is paper, plus a check made out to the Commissioner of Revenue Services.

  • No tax on a principal residence deeded over in lieu of foreclosure.
  • No tax where a principal residence sells for too little to pay the mortgages and the priority liens.
  • No tax on a principal residence with a deteriorated concrete foundation caused by pyrrhotite, if a professional engineer says so and a copy of the evaluation is attached.
  • Estates, trusts and sales with more than two grantors add Schedule A.

Cash cuts out the lender. The price is set from the house in its present state, and the closing date turns on title work and your own schedule. Send us the address and tell us about the condition, and you will get an offer that you are free to refuse.

Houses with postponed work, estate houses and houses with tenants are the usual fits. A buyer who needs a mortgage can stumble over the same problems at inspection or appraisal. When the house is in good order and time is on your side, an agent's listing may do better, and we will tell you so.

1. Locate the deed, and pull your latest mortgage statement and tax bill. The assessor's record shows the build year.
  2. Ask the tax collector whether a fire district charge or any other balance is open.
  3. For an estate or trust sale, confirm who has authority to sign.
  4. Walk the house and write down its known problems, from roof to basement, as plainly as you can.
  5. Engage a closing attorney to run the title search and prepare the OP-236.
  6. Pick a closing date you can actually meet and keep the utilities connected until then.

Bring photo ID and every key on closing day. Payoffs are deducted from your proceeds and you receive the rest. Afterward, save a copy of the recorded deed and the filed return.

sections.h2: From acceptance to the closing table
sections.html:
Once an offer is accepted, a title search checks the record for liens, unpaid taxes and old mortgages that were never discharged. Anything found has to be cleared before the deed passes. The attorney then drafts a closing statement that lists every payoff and charge, so you can see your net before you sign.

With cash, this stretch is mostly the title search and signatures. It runs shorter when the paperwork is clean and longer when an estate or an old lien has to be resolved. If you will be away, ask whether you can sign ahead of time. Tell the buyer about anything unusual in the house, including past water in the basement, and make sure the agreed terms are in writing.

Old kitchens, aging roofs and damp basements do not end a sale, but they decide who buys and on what terms. A buyer with a mortgage faces an appraisal and an inspection, and either one can bring a demand for repairs or a lower price. A cash buyer sees the same flaws and prices them in directly. Which route suits you comes down to how much money, time and patience you can spare.

faqs.a: Fairfield County, as part of the Greater Bridgeport Planning Region.
It covers about 23.5 square miles, and 36,827 people lived there at the 2020 census.

faqs.q: Does Trumbull have a train station?
faqs.a: No, but three Metro-North stations are close: Bridgeport (4.6 miles), Stratford (4.9) and Fairfield-Black Rock (5.7).

faqs.q: Which form goes to the town clerk at a sale?
faqs.a: Form OP-236, the conveyance tax return, filed at recording under Trumbull's town code 144. Your closing attorney can work out the amount.

faqs.q: Must I fix the house before a cash sale?
faqs.a: No. A cash offer takes the property in its current condition.
